text: Claude can't actually run code, check a database, or call a weather service. But it can do something almost as useful: ask you, in structured JSON, to do it on its behalf. That's tool calling, and it's why content was an array of blocks all along.

You describe a tool with a name, a description — which the model actually reads to decide when to reach for it, so write it like real documentation — and an input_schema. That schema is just the JSON Schema from chapter two, reused to describe what arguments the tool accepts.

Ask "what's the weather in San Francisco," and Claude's response carries a tool_use content block: the tool's name, and the input it wants to call it with. Claude never runs get_weather itself — your code reads this block and does the actual lookup.

You run the real lookup, then send the answer back as a new message — a tool_result block, linked to the original call by its tool_use_id. Claude reads that and writes you a real, natural-language answer using it.

So the full round trip, every time: define the tool, Claude replies with a tool_use block, your code actually runs something, and you send a tool_result back. Four steps, and it's the same shape whether you've got one tool or fifty.

Tool calling is the mechanism behind every AI agent that can search, query a database, or take a real action. Next lesson, we handle the less glamorous but equally critical part: what happens when any of this goes wrong.
